title: Taylor v. HCA-HealthONE LLC, 2018 COA 29, 417 P.3d 943
author: Colorado Court of Appeals, Division VI (Harris, J.; Berger, J., concurring in part and dissenting in part)

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source concerns procedural relief after calendaring-software failure, not legal AI’s task-level capabilities, verification requirements, labour effects or workflow redesign. Its recognition that lawyers depend on software that can fail is tangentially relevant to operational risk, but insufficient to establish a position on the cluster’s proposition.
qs: To the contrary, in today's world, lawyers and virtually everyone else (including courts) rely heavily on computer hardware and software to accomplish critical tasks.
But computers fail; either the hardware or the software stops working, sometimes for inexplicable reasons.

st.t: Delegated error: Client relief need not excuse counsel
st.an: Taylor supports the synthesis’s central distinction between counsel’s responsibility and client relief. The majority requires a contextual inquiry into whether software-related neglect was excusable and remands rather than granting automatic relief; Berger more explicitly argues that an innocent client with a meritorious claim should receive relief when defendants face no legal prejudice.
qs: Though she believed the issue had been resolved, some of the dates that appeared to be docketed were not in fact saved in her computer, “despite counsel's efforts.”  ¶ 58 Thus, the question is whether the software malfunction amounted to “unforeseen circumstances,” and whether a reasonably prudent person might have made the same error in relying on docketing software to calendar deadlines.

¶ 93 In those cases in which the fault lies entirely with the lawyer, the plaintiff has a meritorious cause of action, and the defendants will not suffer any legal prejudice if the default judgment or dismissal is vacated, I would conclude that it would be an abuse of discretion not to reinstate the case.

mo.t: Human oversight: Accountability is not effective control
Lawyer accountability: Discipline and liability remain separate
Legal malpractice: Error alone cannot establish liability

kp.k: Calendaring failures allegedly caused a consequential missed service deadline
kp.d: This 2018 decision concerns conventional law-practice software, not AI. Taylor's lawyer attributed missed service deadlines to a calendaring malfunction that deleted entries and only partially restored them. Although the malpractice action was dismissed without prejudice, expiration of the statute of limitations prevented refiling. The account of the malfunction was counsel's explanation, not a definitive appellate finding that technological failure excused the omission.
qs: A technician with whom counsel spoke could not explain why some of the entries were re-entered upon re-enabling of the software, but others were not.
The deadline for obtaining service on Taylor's complaint had been deleted, but not automatically re-entered.
Therefore, despite the district court's dismissal of the lawsuit “without prejudice,” Taylor could not refile the complaint.

kp.k: Excusable neglect requires balancing merits and equity
kp.d: The majority held that the district court applied the wrong legal standard by treating counsel's docketing problems as negligence without considering all three Craig factors: excusability of the neglect, a meritorious claim or defense, and equitable considerations. It vacated the denial of Rule 60(b) relief and remanded for further proceedings rather than directing reinstatement. The governing framework favors adjudication on the merits, especially when relief is requested promptly.
qs: Under Craig, the district court must consider (1) whether the neglect that resulted in entry of judgment was excusable; (2) whether the moving party has alleged a meritorious claim (or defense); and (3) whether relief from the challenged order would be consistent with equitable considerations such as protection of action taken in reliance on the order and prevention of prejudice by reason of evidence lost or impaired by the passage of time.
This rule promotes the long-standing policy favoring resolution of disputes on their merits.
We vacate the district court's order denying Taylor's Rule 60(b) motion and remand the case for further proceedings in accordance with this opinion.

kp.k: Reasonable software reliance requires a contextual factual inquiry
kp.d: The majority distinguished counsel's asserted software malfunction from simply entering deadlines incorrectly. It left the trial court to decide whether the malfunction was unforeseen and whether a reasonably prudent person might similarly rely on the software. This is a conditional standard, not a holding that computer errors automatically establish excusable neglect. The majority also supported a hearing allowing additional evidence rather than confining consideration to counsel's hastily filed initial motion.
qs: Thus, the question is whether the software malfunction amounted to “unforeseen circumstances,” and whether a reasonably prudent person might have made the same error in relying on docketing software to calendar deadlines.
We leave the answer to that question to the district court.
In light of that instruction, we are reluctant to endorse a rule that strictly limits the evidence before the court to the precise information provided in the plaintiff's Rule 60(b) motion.

kp.k: Prompt remediation and actual prejudice shape equitable relief
kp.d: The majority emphasized that Taylor requested relief on the day of dismissal and completed service six or seven days after the court-extended deadline. It directed attention to whether that additional delay impaired defendants' ability to defend the action, rather than treating compliance and noncompliance as reasons for reward or punishment. These were observations to guide the trial court's balancing, not a conclusive majority determination that reinstatement was required.
qs: First, Taylor filed her Rule 60(b) motion as promptly as a party could—on the same day as the dismissal order.
Thus, as we see it, the primary issue is whether the additional six days so prejudiced the defendants’ ability to defend the lawsuit that the equities weigh in favor of dismissal.

If Taylor's failure to follow the rules did not affect the defendants’ course of conduct or compromise their ability to defend against her claims, then the equities favor reinstatement, regardless of the medical center's commendable decision to adhere to applicable deadlines.

kp.k: Berger urged courts to accommodate ordinary computer dependence
kp.d: In his separate concurrence and partial dissent, Judge Berger argued that computer reliance improves efficiency and reduces task time and costs, but failures can occur despite reasonable care. He regarded counsel's uncontradicted explanation as sufficient to establish excusable neglect and would have ordered reinstatement. These technological and remedial conclusions were Berger's position, stronger than the majority's decision to leave the factual assessment open.
qs: That reliance usually benefits everyone because it makes lawyers and others more efficient; computers usually reduce the time necessary to perform a task, and thus reduce costs.
But computers fail; either the hardware or the software stops working, sometimes for inexplicable reasons.
Given the ubiquitous use of computers in law practice and every other aspect of modern life, courts should adjust to the reality that computer failures happen despite a user's reasonable care.
Instead, I would reverse and remand with directions to reinstate the complaint.

kp.k: Berger proposed protecting blameless clients from lawyer negligence
kp.d: Berger criticized uncertainty about attributing lawyers' negligence to clients and the distinction between ordinary and gross negligence. He proposed generally declining to impute lawyer negligence to a blameless client, with reinstatement required when the claim is meritorious and defendants suffer no legal prejudice. He identified competence, diligence, and disciplinary rules as alternatives to penalizing clients. This was a proposed doctrinal approach, not the majority's holding.
qs: Broadening the rule adopted in Coerber, I would generally not impute the lawyer's negligence to the client when the client herself is blameless.
There are other fairer and more effective ways to police lawyers’ competence than visiting lawyers’ sins on their clients.

In those cases in which the fault lies entirely with the lawyer, the plaintiff has a meritorious cause of action, and the defendants will not suffer any legal prejudice if the default judgment or dismissal is vacated, I would conclude that it would be an abuse of discretion not to reinstate the case.

kp.k: Malpractice litigation may inadequately remedy lost client rights
kp.d: In a footnote to his separate opinion, Berger challenged the assumption that a client deprived of a claim by lawyer negligence can obtain adequate compensation through legal malpractice litigation. He stressed the difficulty of proving a case within a case and potentially collectability, preferring relief in the original action when available without prejudice to defendants. This is a judicial argument about client remedies, not an empirical measurement of malpractice recovery rates.
qs: In theory that is true, but in practice it is very difficult for a plaintiff to prevail in a legal malpractice action.
Indeed, the plaintiff must win on a trial within a trial, and may also have to show collectability.
But if a court can give relief to a deserving plaintiff without prejudicing the defendants and thus avoid the necessity of a legal malpractice action, I do not perceive any valid reason not to do so.
